title: Comparing residual error and adjusted R-squared
scenario_markdown: A retailer fits two models to the same 30 stores, with weekly revenue measured in thousands of dollars. Both use an intercept and the same response values (SST=1400). Model A uses floor area (k=1, SSR=840, SSE=560). Model B adds staffing (k=2, SSR=980, SSE=420). Compare their in-sample fit after accounting for predictor count.
assumptions: Both models use the same stores, response units and intercept convention.
Residual standard error uses n-k-1 degrees of freedom.
Fit summaries alone do not establish causation or future prediction quality.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is Model A's residual standard error, in thousands of dollars? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Use residual df n-k-1, not n.
MSE is in squared response units; take its square root.

stages.explanation_markdown: $s_e=\sqrt{560/(30-1-1)}=\sqrt{20}$. Excel: `=SQRT(560/28)`. It measures residual dispersion in the response units.

stages.prompt_markdown: What is Model B's adjusted R-squared (a proportion)? Select the value rounded to four decimal places.

options.hint_markdown: Ordinary R-squared does not penalize predictor count.
SSE/SST is unexplained variation before adjustment.

options.text_markdown: B has lower residual standard error and higher adjusted R-squared; validate future prediction separately.
A must fit better because it has fewer predictors.
options.hint_markdown: Simplicity matters through the penalty, but compare the actual adjusted metrics.

options.text_markdown: B is guaranteed to predict every future store more accurately.
options.hint_markdown: In-sample fit does not guarantee generalization.

stages.explanation_markdown: A has adjusted R-squared 0.5857 and residual SE 4.4721; B has adjusted R-squared 0.6778 and residual SE 3.9441. These favor B for these fit criteria. Held-out performance and subject knowledge still matter.
